THE CROWNWING CARE LIBRARY

Choosing a parrot for your home

A practical starting point for comparing species, routines, noise, space and long-term care.

Start with your routine, not a favourite photograph

Write down what an ordinary week looks like, including work, travel and time away from home. Identify who will provide feeding, cleaning, enrichment and interaction. A sustainable routine should work beyond weekends and the first few weeks.

Then consider the household. Noise tolerance, usable space, other animals and the expectations of everyone living with the bird can change which species are appropriate. Make these decisions before narrowing the shortlist.

Compare exact species

Group names are helpful for browsing, but they do not describe identical needs. Small and large macaws differ substantially; parakeets include birds with very different adult sizes and lifespans. Use the parrot collection to explore groups, then ask about the exact species.

Compare diet, accommodation, vocalisation and long-term commitment together. A smaller bird is not automatically a quiet or low-maintenance bird, and talking ability should not be treated as an essential feature.

Meet the individual through better questions

Ask what the bird enjoys, what makes it uncomfortable and how it reacts to unfamiliar people. Request an explanation of its current routine and the information available about its history. Ask for recent photographs or video and distinguish documented facts from assumptions.

Behaviour is influenced by environment and experience. A label such as “friendly” cannot guarantee that a bird will immediately behave the same way in your home. Allow room for gradual adjustment.

Build a shortlist you can support

Select two or three possibilities and compare the real daily requirements. Consider what would happen if your working hours changed or you needed someone else to care for the bird. Review ongoing ownership costs as well as purchase price.

Before making a commitment, work through the buying checklist and home preparation guide. A sensible match should remain practical even when the bird is vocal, independent or uninterested in talking.

Compare a shortlist against ordinary life

Once you have two or three possible species, compare the same practical details for each rather than trying to name an overall winner. Write down the space you can safely provide, the household’s tolerance for vocalisation, the time available for social contact and supervised activity, and who can maintain the routine when your week changes. Consider expected lifespan and the possibility that care arrangements will need to outlast your present home, job or family circumstances. There is no universal “best parrot”: suitability is a match between an individual bird’s needs and a household’s realistic capacity.

Talking is not guaranteed, and a bird that vocalises less in one setting may behave differently after moving or as its routine changes. Ask whether you can accept a companion whose main communication is not speech. Likewise, a young age, hand-rearing or a description such as “tame” cannot promise a particular temperament. Ask about the actual bird’s history, what interactions it chooses and how it responds to unfamiliar people. Plan to build trust gradually and positively rather than expecting a label to predict behaviour.

Finally, test your shortlist against its care requirements: suitable housing and enrichment, a stable diet, veterinary access, costs, other animals and time away from home. Use the housing guide, nutrition guide and ownership-cost guide to identify questions to resolve. Then check what is known about the individual bird; a general species profile cannot establish its exact needs or current availability.

Try a “difficult day” test before choosing: if your bird is unsettled, louder than expected or uninterested in interaction, can the household respond patiently without punishment or neglecting other responsibilities? Include a realistic plan for holidays, a change in work pattern and veterinary appointments. If an arrangement you rely on has not been confirmed, treat it as an open question rather than an assumption.

Keep notes on what evidence you still need for each shortlisted species and individual. This makes a future seller conversation more useful. If no option fits your home now, waiting and revisiting the decision after practical changes is a responsible outcome.

A considered shortlist

Compare the day-to-day, not a score

Use this guide to start a conversation about the exact species and individual. Group descriptions are broad context, not a prediction of any one bird.

There is variation between species and individual birds within every group. Talking is never guaranteed. No group is ranked here, and this comparison does not indicate current availability.

Agree responsibilities and usable space

Check the same practical questions with every person who shares the home. Who supplies meals and water, cleans equipment, supervises activity and notices changes in appetite or behaviour? Who can take over if the usual keeper is delayed? Agreement should cover the ordinary routine, not just enthusiasm for a new companion.

Measure usable room with the planned enclosure, perches and household furniture in place. Identify where supervised movement can happen and how doors, windows and other animals will be managed. In shared accommodation, discuss vocalisation and any tenancy restrictions before choosing an individual. A compact bird still needs movement and social opportunities; limited room is not solved merely by buying the smallest cage.

Test a normal week and a difficult week

  • Ordinary days: write down who provides familiar care, safe exercise and suitable interaction before and after work or study.
  • Busy days: identify which responsibilities must still happen when plans change. A toy purchase is not a substitute for supervision and care.
  • Time away: confirm a willing, capable backup keeper and whether the accommodation and familiar routine can remain suitable.
  • Unexpected changes: decide who can contact the veterinary practice, arrange a journey or maintain care if the usual keeper is unavailable.

Use this plan to compare needs, not to set a universal number of hours for every parrot. If the plan relies on unconfirmed help, mark it as unresolved. Put any additional care costs into the ownership budget.

Check first-time expectations against the individual

Write down what you expect from handling, vocalisation and companionship, then ask the current keeper what is actually known. Can the household accept a bird that does not talk, prefers limited touch or takes time to trust unfamiliar people? Labels such as young, hand-reared or tame do not answer those questions.

Separate a wish from a requirement the household cannot accommodate. Discuss the identified species and individual rather than choosing from photographs alone. Waiting is preferable to relying on a routine, space or temperament assumption that has not been resolved.
